narr: Let's dive into the first set of grammar exercises from English for Engineering I.
We'll explore some common verb tenses and quantification rules used in everyday English.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Verb Tenses
data.problem: Could you help me? I (try) to translate this letter from a Spanish client and I don't know what this word (mean).

steps.text: The first action 'try' is ongoing, so it needs the continuous form.
The second action 'mean' is a stative verb showing a state, so it needs the simple form.

narr: Let's look at our first problem.
The speaker is in the middle of trying to translate a letter.
So we need the continuous form 'am trying' for the first blank.
For the second blank, 'mean' is a stative verb describing a state of knowing.
Therefore, it takes the simple form 'means'.

data.heading: Problem 2 — Verb Tenses
data.problem: I (apply) for a transfer to our London office, but I don't know if I'll be successful. It all (depend) on whether or not they have any vacancies.

steps.text: The first action 'apply' is ongoing, so it needs the continuous form.
The second action 'depend' is a stative verb showing a state, so it needs the simple form.

narr: Next problem involves applying for a transfer.
The action of applying is still in progress, so we use 'am applying'.
The outcome 'depends' on vacancies, which is a stative state.
So we use the simple form 'depends'.

data.heading: Problem 3 — Verb Tenses
data.problem: Their new 'own brand' instant coffee (taste) very good, so it isn't surprising that it (become) more and more popular.

steps.text: The first action 'taste' describes a quality, so it's a stative verb needing the simple form.
The second action 'become' is ongoing and changing, so it needs the continuous form.

narr: For our third problem, we're talking about coffee.
The taste of coffee is a quality or state, so we use the simple form 'tastes'.
The popularity is increasing over time, so we use the continuous form 'is becoming'.

data.heading: Key Rule: Continuous vs. Simple
items: Action in progress → continuous (carry out, try, do, apply, become)
Stative meaning → simple (want, sound, know, mean, depend, taste)

narr: Let's recap the key rule here.
When an action is ongoing or in progress, we use the continuous tense.
When we're describing a state or quality, we use the simple tense.
This is Rule 4 from Week 2, and it's a classic test question trap.
Now let's move on to Week 3, which focuses on quantification.
We'll cover both the grammar of quantifiers and the language of numbers.

data.heading: Quantifiers with Countable and Uncountable Nouns
bullets: Countable nouns: can be counted (one chair, two chairs, three chairs)
Uncountable nouns: cannot be counted individually (water, furniture, information)
Different quantifiers are used with each type

narr: First, let's understand the difference between countable and uncountable nouns.
Countable nouns are things we can count individually, like chairs or tigers.
Uncountable nouns are things we can't count individually, like water or information.
This distinction is crucial because it determines which quantifiers we use.

data.heading: Key Quantifiers
bullets: no/none: zero quantity
all/whole: complete quantity
each/every: individual members
both: two things together
either/neither: one or the other / neither one

narr: Let's explore some key quantifiers used in English.
First, we have 'no' and 'none' which indicate zero quantity.
Next, 'all' and 'whole' refer to a complete quantity.
Then we have 'each' and 'every' which refer to individual members of a group.
For two things, we use 'both' to refer to them together.
Finally, 'either' means one or the other, while 'neither' means not one or the other.

data.heading: Quantifier Usage Examples
bullets: no — with a noun to describe zero quantity: No animal can live for long without water.
none of — to mean 'not one' of a group: None of the students had done the work.
none — to mean 'not any' or 'not one': There was none left. (singular verb)
all (of) — with a plural noun and verb: All animals need water to live.
most (of) — to mean 'nearly all': Most mammals have hair.

narr: Let's look at some examples of how these quantifiers are used.
First, 'no' is used with a noun to describe zero quantity.
Next, 'none of' means 'not one' of a specific group.
When used alone, 'none' means 'not any' and takes a singular verb.
For complete quantity, we use 'all' with plural nouns and verbs.
When we mean 'nearly all', we use 'most'.

data.heading: More Quantifier Examples
bullets: each (of) — the separate members of a group: We put 50 cc of water in each test tube.
every — with a singular noun, to mean all members together: Every person in the class took part.
whole — to mean 'all of something': You'd better tell me the whole story.
both (of) — to refer to two things: Both books were written in 1985.
either (of) — to mean 'this or the other': Either method will give results.

narr: Continuing with more quantifier examples.
Each refers to separate members of a group, like water in each test tube.
Every refers to all members together, taking a singular noun.
Whole means 'all of something' as a complete unit.
Both is used for exactly two things.
Either means one or the other of two options.

data.heading: Final Quantifier Examples
bullets: neither (of) — to mean 'not this or the other': Neither of the answers is correct.
Large quantities: a lot of/lots of in affirmative sentences
Small quantities: a few/a little in positive statements
Very small quantities: few/little in negative statements
Excessive quantities: too many/too much

narr: Let's finish with our last quantifier examples.
Neither means not one or the other of two options.
For large quantities, we use 'a lot of' or 'lots of' in positive statements.
For small quantities, we use 'a few' for countables and 'a little' for uncountables.
In negative statements, we use 'few' and 'little' for very small quantities.
When we have excessive amounts, we use 'too many' for countables and 'too much' for uncountables.

rows.text: how many
questions about quantity with countable nouns
How many tigers are there in the world today?
how much
questions about mass with uncountable nouns
How much water is there on Earth?
not many
negative statement about quantity of countables
There aren't many tigers left in the world today.
not much
negative statement about mass of uncountables
There isn't much time left to save the tigers.
many/much
positive statements in formal or written language
Many people hunt wild animals. Much damage has been caused.

narr: Now let's look at a comprehensive table of quantity expressions.
First, we have 'how many' for questions about countable nouns.
Next, 'how much' is used for questions about uncountable nouns.
For negative statements about countables, we use 'not many'.
For negative statements about uncountables, we use 'not much'.
In formal or written language, we use 'many' and 'much' for positive statements.

rows.text: a few
a small number of countables in a positive way
We managed to see a few tigers in the distance.
a little
a small amount of an uncountable in a positive way
There is a little water left in this bottle.
a lot (of), lots (of)
a large number of countables or a large amount of an uncountable
We saw a lot of animals close up. There was a lot of rain last month.
few, very few, only a few
countables in a negative way
Few conservationists believe tigers have a future. There are only a few biscuits left.
little, very little, only a little
uncountables in a negative way
There is little hope that tigers will survive. There is only a little water left.

narr: Continuing with more quantity expressions.
A few indicates a small number of countables in a positive context.
A little indicates a small amount of an uncountable in a positive context.
A lot of or lots of indicate large quantities of either countables or uncountables.
When we have very few countables in a negative context, we use 'few', 'very few', or 'only a few'.
Similarly, for very little uncountable in a negative context, we use 'little', 'very little', or 'only a little'.

rows.text: too many
countables — more things than are necessary or possible
There are too many stars for scientists to count.
too much
uncountables — a greater quantity than is necessary or possible
Some plants are damaged by too much sunlight.
enough (of)
the quantity or number is sufficient
Have we got enough food? There are enough plates for everyone.
not enough
the quantity or number is not sufficient
There is not enough information about this problem.
plenty of
more than enough
Don't worry, we have plenty of time. I've got plenty of pens if you need one.

narr: Let's finish with our final set of quantity expressions.
Too many indicates an excessive number of countables.
Too much indicates an excessive amount of uncountables.
Enough indicates that the quantity is sufficient.
Not enough indicates that the quantity is insufficient.
Plenty of indicates that there is more than enough.
